ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The PPMI study and Verily Study Watch substudy were approved by the relevant institutional review boards or ethics committees at participating sites, and all participants provided written informed consent.

The AI-PROGNOSIS dBM-DEV study was approved by the relevant ethics committees at participating sites (Germany: Ethikkommission an der TU Dresden -BO-EK-2012024; France: Comité de protection des personnes Ile de France III -2023-A02136-59; Spain: Comité de Ética de la Investigación con medicamentos del Hospital Ruber Internacional de Madrid -Sa-18773 / 15 -EC: 535), and all participants provided written informed consent.

table.text: The Verily Study Watch substudy was conducted in the U.S. from 2018 to 2020, and participants were monitored using the Verily Study Watch (Verily Life Sciences LLC, Dallas, TX, USA).

The dBM-DEV study was conducted in Germany, France, and Spain between October 2024 and January 2026, and participants were monitored using the Garmin Vivoactive 5 smartwatch (Garmin Ltd., Schaffhausen, Switzerland).

After applying the weartime inclusion criteria, 283 participants from the Verily Study Watch cohort (133 PwPD, 26 HCs, 124 atrisk individuals) and 61 participants from the dBM-DEV study cohort (20 PwPD, 20 HCs, 21 at-risk individuals) qualified for further analysis.

> The Verily Study Watch substudy was conducted in the U.S. from 2018 to 2020, and participants were monitored using the Verily Study Watch (Verily Life Sciences LLC, Dallas, TX, USA).

> The dBM-DEV study was conducted in Germany, France, and Spain between October 2024 and January 2026, and participants were monitored using the Garmin Vivoactive 5 smartwatch (Garmin Ltd., Schaffhausen, Switzerland).

> After applying the weartime inclusion criteria, 283 participants from the Verily Study Watch cohort (133 PwPD, 26 HCs, 124 atrisk individuals) and 61 participants from the dBM-DEV study cohort (20 PwPD, 20 HCs, 21 at-risk individuals) qualified for further analysis.

> The PPMI study and Verily Study Watch substudy were approved by the relevant institutional review boards or ethics committees at participating sites, and all participants provided written informed consent.

> The AI-PROGNOSIS dBM-DEV study was approved by the relevant ethics committees at participating sites (Germany: Ethikkommission an der TU Dresden -BO-EK-2012024; France: Comité de protection des personnes Ile de France III -2023-A02136-59; Spain: Comité de Ética de la Investigación con medicamentos del Hospital Ruber Internacional de Madrid -Sa-18773 / 15 -EC: 535), and all participants provided written informed consent.

> Values were imputed using sex-and age-specific national reference means [36] for four participants and sexspecific dBM-DEV cohort means for the remaining one.

> For the classification analysis, participants were categorized as having normal dopaminergic function or dopaminergic deficit based on their DAT scan result.

> For the classification analysis, participants were categorized as having αsynuclein pathology based on a positive SAA result or not having α-synuclein pathology based on a negative SAA result, regardless of assay protocol.

> In the both-hallmark analysis, participants were considered positive if they had an abnormal DAT scan and a positive SAA result.

> In the maximum score approach, participants were classified as positive (having one, either, or both pathologies) if either score exceeded its respective decision threshold.

> In the sequential screening approach, participants were classified as positive only if both scores exceeded their respective decision thresholds.

> For inclusion in the MDS prodromal PD risk score, participants were subsequently classified into high-or low-PRS categories using quartile thresholds derived from the PRS distribution in the unified Accelerating Medicines Partnership Parkinson's disease (AMP-PD) cohorts [51].

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}

"p < 0.05", "p < 0.05", "p < 0.05", "p < 0.05", "p < 0.05"),
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p ≥ 0.197", "p = 0.06"), Sentence = c("No statistical differences in sex, age, or body mass index (BMI) were observed between PwPD and HCs in either cohort (p ≥ 0.197).", "The SAM-PD score showed a moderate positive correlation with the MDS risk score (r = 0.43, p < 0.05) and a weak, non-significant positive correlation with the mini-MDS risk score (r = 0.17, p = 0.06)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

live_data_statements: The demographic and clinical characteristics of included participants are summarized in Table 1.
In the PwPD group, 85 of 86 participants had an abnormal DAT scan (98.8%) and 105 of 122 had a positive SAA test (86.1%).

In the combined PwPD and HC cohort (Fig. 3a), higher SAM-PD scores were associated with lower SBR (Pearson r = -0.60, p < 0.05, n = 112) and higher SAA mean Fmax (r = +0.48, p < 0.05, n = 128); 20 of 148 participants were excluded from the Fmax correlation analysis, because their SAA results were obtained using a different assay protocol.
The Verily Study Watch substudy was conducted in the U.S. from 2018 to 2020, and participants were monitored using the Verily Study Watch (Verily Life Sciences LLC, Dallas, TX, USA).

The dBM-DEV study was conducted in Germany, France, and Spain between October 2024 and January 2026, and participants were monitored using the Garmin Vivoactive 5 smartwatch (Garmin Ltd., Schaffhausen, Switzerland).

After applying the weartime inclusion criteria, 283 participants from the Verily Study Watch cohort (133 PwPD, 26 HCs, 124 atrisk individuals) and 61 participants from the dBM-DEV study cohort (20 PwPD, 20 HCs, 21 at-risk individuals) qualified for further analysis.

The PPMI study and Verily Study Watch substudy were approved by the relevant institutional review boards or ethics committees at participating sites, and all participants provided written informed consent.

The AI-PROGNOSIS dBM-DEV study was approved by the relevant ethics committees at participating sites (Germany: Ethikkommission an der TU Dresden -BO-EK-2012024; France: Comité de protection des personnes Ile de France III -2023-A02136-59; Spain: Comité de Ética de la Investigación con medicamentos del Hospital Ruber Internacional de Madrid -Sa-18773 / 15 -EC: 535), and all participants provided written informed consent.
Values were imputed using sex-and age-specific national reference means [36] for four participants and sexspecific dBM-DEV cohort means for the remaining one.
For the classification analysis, participants were categorized as having normal dopaminergic function or dopaminergic deficit based on their DAT scan result.

For the classification analysis, participants were categorized as having αsynuclein pathology based on a positive SAA result or not having α-synuclein pathology based on a negative SAA result, regardless of assay protocol.
In the both-hallmark analysis, participants were considered positive if they had an abnormal DAT scan and a positive SAA result.
In the maximum score approach, participants were classified as positive (having one, either, or both pathologies) if either score exceeded its respective decision threshold.
In the sequential screening approach, participants were classified as positive only if both scores exceeded their respective decision thresholds.

For inclusion in the MDS prodromal PD risk score, participants were subsequently classified into high-or low-PRS categories using quartile thresholds derived from the PRS distribution in the unified Accelerating Medicines Partnership Parkinson's disease (AMP-PD) cohorts [51].
In each LOSO fold, SHAP values for the held-out participant were computed with the same fitted model that generated their prediction.
